Alaskan Murders

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
He was an unsuspecting South African, building a new life in Alaska. Then he confessed to two grisly murders, which he documented for the Dark Web.

Unique Selling Point:
In February 2024, an Alaskan court found Brian Steven Smith (52) guilty of 14 charges - including two counts of murder, sexual assault, and torture.
To the outside world, Brianwas your quintessential ‘nice guy’ - pleasant, quiet, standoffish, and awkward at times but his colleagues put that down to him being a non-Alaskan native.
But behind closed doors, he was a man who frequently spoke of his deeply-rooted racist beliefs, was a regular on depraved chat sites on the dark web, and made snuff films.

This is a story of the ‘meek’ man turned murderer, who left South Africa to pursue love, and now finds himself facing two life sentences for two brutal murders.

Summary:
Brian Steven Smith, originally from Komani in the Eastern Cape, awaits sentencing for the murders of two native Alaskan women in Anchorage, Alaska in 2018 and 2019 respectively.
Now experts believe he may be connected to a series of unsolved murders in SA after he confessed to more killings.
Brian documented one of his murders - making 12 videos and taking 39 pictures of himself raping, torturing and murdering one of his victims.
He narrated his actions in the videos as if to an audience, saying: "In my movies, people always die," and "People need to know when they're being serial-killed."

This story will delve into the man behind the murders, looking at Brian's life growing up and living in the Eastern Cape, as well as his online persona. It will also tell the stories of his victims, and the families they've now left behind.



Further information:
Sentencing is scheduled for July 12 and 19. He faces 30 to 99 years behind bars for killing Abouchuk, but will get the mandatory maximum of 99 years in prison for Henry’s death because jurors determined that there was an aggravating factor: He subjected her to substantial physical torture.

Press Release:


Memory Card Murders:
It was a case out of Alaska in the United States that gained international attention back in 2019: the discovery of a memory card containing footage of a brutal murder. The man behind the horrific crime was South African, Brian Steven Smith, a newly naturalised US citizen who had documented himself strangling a native Alaskan woman to death in a hotel room. He’d later confess to the murder of another Alaskan woman a year earlier. In February, Smith was convicted on 14 charges, including two counts of murder. He now awaits his fate in a US jail. Carte Blanche tracks his journey from the streets of Komani in the Eastern Cape to his gruesome murders in Alaska.

Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Erin Bates

Script:



OPENING MONTAGE: NEWS FOOTAGE
BRIAN AUDIO: ‘You live. You die. You live. You die. You die. Sadly, in my movies, everyone dies.’

VO:
It reads like a thriller….

A stolen cellphone with evidence of cold-hearted brutality…

A sadistic killer…

And.. an inter-continental investigation into a trail of bodies…


VO:
But this isn’t fiction; it’s the true story of the so-called ‘Alaskan Memory Card Murders’…

And the South African man accused of them, now awaiting his fate in a U.S. prison.

VO:
Five years ago, Alaska’s capital, Anchorage, was the scene of a gruesome crime.

A 48-year-old man was arrested for the torture and murder of a 30-year-old native Alaskan woman after a memory card was handed to the police. It was ominously labeled ‘Homicide at midtown Marriott’.

On it: haunting images and videos of the victim’s final moments.

POLICE LIVE FOOTAGE

VO:
The accused was South African, Brian Steven Smith, a naturalised U.S. citizen who had moved to Alaska in 2014.

VO:
The evidence presented in a trial that ended in February, was stomach-churning… a grotesque story of murder captured for posterity.

A story that begins in the dusty streets of Komani in the Eastern Cape, a place Smith once called home.

LINK:
“Those who knew him growing up in this street on Maple Crescent, say Smith was soft spoken and mild mannered, more comfortable working on computers than around people. [PAUSE] One relative told us he was always on the fringes.”

VO: She’s an immediate family member we’ll call Maria to protect her identity. Since his arrest she’s received death threats and is worried about her safety.

ERIN: ‘What can you tell me about his childhood, his upbringing, his roots essentially?’

ZITA: “Eastern Cape, born and bred. It was a normal childhood by any description. Mom. Dad, the dog, the house, the everything - there was nothing unusual about the upbringing… there was nothing as I can say that would have led us to believe this is where Brian is going to end up, this is what is going to happen to Brian - not at all.”



ERIN: “Why did you choose to speak to Carte Blanche about Brian?”

ZITA: “All I’ve tried to do is not make excuses for him, not protect him, but maybe just give a little bit of a background that he was someone’s child, and someone’s brother, and someone’s husband. And that not everyone is born a monster.”

VO:
The victim was Kathleen-Jo Henry, a homeless Alaskan woman who’d been reported missing in 2019.

Smith had taken her to a local hotel, the Midtown Marriott, tortured her for two days and then strangled her to death.
He discarded her body along a nearby highway.

SMITH:
“Listen, you need to finish this movie, because I just can’t (expletive) go on anymore. Gasp once for yes, gasp twice for no.”

VO:
During the three-week trial, the jury watched all 12 videos of Henry’s murder.
Smith didn’t show his face… but narrated his savagery.

SMITH:
“Do people have to be taught how to die these days? Oh (expletive). Hundred and twenty years of (expletive) evolution and you haven’t learnt to die yet? (expletive) bitch. I don’t have (expletive) time for your shit.”

ERIN: ‘Did you hear some of the audio from the recordings?’
ZITA: “yes, yes…”
ERIN: ‘What was that like? Did you know the voice of that man?’
ZITA: “I knew the voice, I didn’t know the vocabulary. I remember speaking to his sister and saying ‘it can’t be’... To taunt someone when they are busy… Yeah, it was horrific. That hit me solidly. There was no getting away from it. He was as guilty as guilty can be.

VO:
The depravity of his actions stands in contrast to the man described by many as ‘mild-mannered’ and ‘quiet’.

LINK:
‘’At 42, Smith packed up his life in sunny South Africa and emigrated to cold, unfamiliar Alaska in the United States. He emigrated "for love" and married a woman some 20 years his senior he met online.’’

VO:
That woman was Stephanie Bissland, a former US government employee.

The pair met in 2013, and by 2014 Smith was married and living in Alaska, working odd jobs to make ends meet.

VO:
Bissland supported her husband in court but has since filed for divorce.

VO:
Their relationship may have appeared idyllic, but the investigation revealed a different picture: during interrogation by the police, Smith admitted to infidelity when describing how he’d murdered another woman a year earlier. This time, in his own house.

SMITH: “Yeah, I just shot her, I just shot the gun. There was no… The only messed up thing I can tell you guys honestly there was no emotion, it was just: ‘You’re not listening to me, go shower, you’re not…’

VO:
That victim was Veronica Abouchuk, another indigenous Alaskan and mother-of-four. Like Henry she had a history of homelessness.
Her body was also dumped along a highway with a bullet-wound to the skull.

VO:
It’s an instinct for violence those who knew him say seems completely out of character.

Footage of Smith at the lake.

LINK: “Smith attended prestigious Queen's College for junior and high school. In Standard 9, what's now called Grade 11, he moved to a nearby technical college where he completed matric. Then, he did military service - in Bloemfontein.”

VO:
Not much is known about what happened after that. It’s believed Smith drifted from place to place, moving from job to job.

Wayne van Straaten is a childhood friend.

ERIN: ‘Sitting next to him at school, what was he like?? What was his personality like?’
WAYNE: “A very nice person, fun, makes jokes, smiling…

WAYNE: “When we did IQ tests in junior school, Brian came out with the highest IQ in the grade. He’s a very smart guy, I think he can manipulate things.”

ERIN: ‘Do you think he had the kind of IQ that might let him get away literally with murder in South Africa?’

WAYNE: “Well I think so, because what we’ve seen now is how he fooled all of us, so I don’t see how he couldn’t get away with it in South Africa.”

VO:
Smith was eventually made to account for his crimes in Alaska thanks to convicted criminal, drug addict, sex worker… and key witness… Valerie Casler.

VO:
In October 2019, Smith paid her for sex.

PROSECUTOR: ‘What specifically stood out about the man to you, as far as physical features or voice?’
VALERIE: “His accent.”
PROSECUTOR: ‘And what was it? Describe it?’
VALERIE: “It sounded like European or something.”

VO: As they stopped at an ATM, she stole Smith’s cellphone and fled, not knowing its shocking contents or how it would become instrumental in his conviction.

PAUSE
Casler transferred the footage to a memory card and handed it to police.

Detective 1: ‘You know what you did in that video?’
Brian: “Yes, uhm. I, I did not realise this, I did not know this.”
Detective 2: ‘You’re still saying that you didn’t know, that that that…’

Detective 1: ‘Well this is you.’
Brian: “And, and I’m on camera on that.”
Detective 1: ‘If you are…’
Brian: “I can’t get out of it. You’ve got evidence on me. I’m going to the chair…”

VO:
During the trial, a picture emerged of a man who took pleasure in recording the torture of his victims… even describing himself as a ‘serial killer’.

WAYNE: “When I look at pictures of him on the news channels, his eyes are just - they've got this wild look in them. It’s not the look I know. It’s not the same person. He just looks angry, aggressive, and that’s not the person that I knew.”

LINK: “Kathleen Jo Henry and Veronica Abouchak died senseless deaths at Smith's hand, in the place of their birth, Alaska. But an alleged jail cell confession brings the saga right back to his homeland.”


VO:
Adrian Pillay worked with Smith at an IT firm in Johannesburg for two years, and the pair remained friends.


In 2019 he was interrogated by police over Smith’s criminal history in South Africa.


ADRIAN ZOOM:
“When I did get interviewed by the police, I had to go to Pretoria to speak to them. I asked them ‘why?’ Why they were interviewing me? And they said Brian had allegedly told his cellmates when he was in the US that he had murdered many women and he had never been caught.”


ERIN: ‘Are you aware that the American authorities as well as the SAPS have spent some time and care looking into his record here?’
ZITA: “Yes…”
ERIN: ‘And that there is a suspicion based reportedly on a confession that he himself made that his criminality began in SA…?’
ZITA: “I wasn’t aware of that.”
ERIN: ‘Does it surprise you if I told you that is a fact?’
ZITA: “I think at this stage, nothing surprises me. Honestly, nothing surprises me.
ZITA: “I have no answers. He - he was either beyond confident, maybe he wanted to be caught…

VO:
In February this year, almost five years after his arrest, a jury convicted Smith on 14 charges, including murder, and sexual assault.

ERIN: ‘Do you still love Brian, and can you forgive him?’

ZITA: “I can’t answer that now, I’ve got to be honest with you.”



VO:
The families of Smith’s victims now await justice: he’ll be sentenced for his crime later this month.

ZITA: “Brian didn’t just kill two women - the impact on everyone went beyond those two women. As a family, we have so much - how can I put it - their families have lost so much, but we’ve also lost someone - because we lost the Brian we knew. This isn't Brian. It’s not Brian.”

ZITA: “Honestly… the only way Brian will leave prison is in a box, it’s that simple.”


—------------------------------

PRESENTER: He's been convicted of the so-called memory card murders in Anchorage, Alaska. But police suspect, it doesn't end there.

PRESENTER: An alleged jail cell confession has authorities looking into long forgotten cold cases in SA.

PRESENTER: A South African convicted of two gruesome murders in Anchorage, Alaska awaits sentencing...

BYTE

PRESENTER: We track his origins in the Eastern Cape and trace the makings of a murderer in the United States.

PRESENTER: Found guilty of two murders in Alaska, the United States... The culprit was born here in rural Eastern Cape...

PRESENTER: What drove him to commit cold-blooded murder 17,000 kilometres away? And what trail of secrets did he leave in South Africa?

Dad, the dog, the house, the everything - there was nothing unusual about the upbringing… there was nothing as I can say that would have led us to believe this is where Brian is going to end up, this is what is going to happen to Brian - not at all.” ERIN: “Why did you choose to speak to Carte Blanche about Brian?” ZITA: “All I’ve tried to do is not make excuses for him, not protect him, but maybe just give a little bit of a background that he was someone’s child, and someone’s brother, and someone’s husband. And that not everyone is born a monster.” VO: The victim was Kathleen-Jo Henry, a homeless Alaskan woman who’d been reported missing in 2019. Smith had taken her to a local hotel, the Midtown Marriott, tortured her for two days and then strangled her to death. He discarded her body along a nearby highway. SMITH: “Listen, you need to finish this movie, because I just can’t (expletive) go on anymore. Gasp once for yes, gasp twice for no.” VO: During the three-week trial, the jury watched all 12 videos of Henry’s murder. Smith didn’t show his face… but narrated his savagery. SMITH: “Do people have to be taught how to die these days? Oh (expletive). Hundred and twenty years of (expletive) evolution and you haven’t learnt to die yet? (expletive) bitch. I don’t have (expletive) time for your shit.” ERIN: ‘Did you hear some of the audio from the recordings?’ ZITA: “yes, yes…” ERIN: ‘What was that like? Did you know the voice of that man?’ ZITA: “I knew the voice, I didn’t know the vocabulary. I remember speaking to his sister and saying ‘it can’t be’... To taunt someone when they are busy… Yeah, it was horrific. That hit me solidly. There was no getting away from it. He was as guilty as guilty can be. VO: The depravity of his actions stands in contrast to the man described by many as ‘mild-mannered’ and ‘quiet’. LINK: ‘’At 42, Smith packed up his life in sunny South Africa and emigrated to cold, unfamiliar Alaska in the United States. He emigrated "for love" and married a woman some 20 years his senior he met online.’’ VO: That woman was Stephanie Bissland, a former US government employee. The pair met in 2013, and by 2014 Smith was married and living in Alaska, working odd jobs to make ends meet. VO: Bissland supported her husband in court but has since filed for divorce. VO: Their relationship may have appeared idyllic, but the investigation revealed a different picture: during interrogation by the police, Smith admitted to infidelity when describing how he’d murdered another woman a year earlier. This time, in his own house. SMITH: “Yeah, I just shot her, I just shot the gun. There was no… The only messed up thing I can tell you guys honestly there was no emotion, it was just: ‘You’re not listening to me, go shower, you’re not…’ VO: That victim was Veronica Abouchuk, another indigenous Alaskan and mother-of-four. Like Henry she had a history of homelessness. Her body was also dumped along a highway with a bullet-wound to the skull. VO: It’s an instinct for violence those who knew him say seems completely out of character. Footage of Smith at the lake. LINK: “Smith attended prestigious Queen's College for junior and high school. In Standard 9, what's now called Grade 11, he moved to a nearby technical college where he completed matric. Then, he did military service - in Bloemfontein.” VO: Not much is known about what happened after that. It’s believed Smith drifted from place to place, moving from job to job. Wayne van Straaten is a childhood friend. ERIN: ‘Sitting next to him at school, what was he like?? What was his personality like?’ WAYNE: “A very nice person, fun, makes jokes, smiling… WAYNE: “When we did IQ tests in junior school, Brian came out with the highest IQ in the grade. He’s a very smart guy, I think he can manipulate things.” ERIN: ‘Do you think he had the kind of IQ that might let him get away literally with murder in South Africa?’ WAYNE: “Well I think so, because what we’ve seen now is how he fooled all of us, so I don’t see how he couldn’t get away with it in South Africa.” VO: Smith was eventually made to account for his crimes in Alaska thanks to convicted criminal, drug addict, sex worker… and key witness… Valerie Casler. VO: In October 2019, Smith paid her for sex. PROSECUTOR: ‘What specifically stood out about the man to you, as far as physical features or voice?’ VALERIE: “His accent.” PROSECUTOR: ‘And what was it? Describe it?’ VALERIE: “It sounded like European or something.” VO: As they stopped at an ATM, she stole Smith’s cellphone and fled, not knowing its shocking contents or how it would become instrumental in his conviction. PAUSE Casler transferred the footage to a memory card and handed it to police. Detective 1: ‘You know what you did in that video?’ Brian: “Yes, uhm. I, I did not realise this, I did not know this.” Detective 2: ‘You’re still saying that you didn’t know, that that that…’ Detective 1: ‘Well this is you.’ Brian: “And, and I’m on camera on that.” Detective 1: ‘If you are…’ Brian: “I can’t get out of it. You’ve got evidence on me. I’m going to the chair…” VO: During the trial, a picture emerged of a man who took pleasure in recording the torture of his victims… even describing himself as a ‘serial killer’. WAYNE: “When I look at pictures of him on the news channels, his eyes are just - they've got this wild look in them. It’s not the look I know. It’s not the same person. He just looks angry, aggressive, and that’s not the person that I knew.” LINK: “Kathleen Jo Henry and Veronica Abouchak died senseless deaths at Smith's hand, in the place of their birth, Alaska. But an alleged jail cell confession brings the saga right back to his homeland.” VO: Adrian Pillay worked with Smith at an IT firm in Johannesburg for two years, and the pair remained friends. In 2019 he was interrogated by police over Smith’s criminal history in South Africa. ADRIAN ZOOM: “When I did get interviewed by the police, I had to go to Pretoria to speak to them. I asked them ‘why?’ Why they were interviewing me? And they said Brian had allegedly told his cellmates when he was in the US that he had murdered many women and he had never been caught.” ERIN: ‘Are you aware that the American authorities as well as the SAPS have spent some time and care looking into his record here?’ ZITA: “Yes…” ERIN: ‘And that there is a suspicion based reportedly on a confession that he himself made that his criminality began in SA…?’ ZITA: “I wasn’t aware of that.” ERIN: ‘Does it surprise you if I told you that is a fact?’ ZITA: “I think at this stage, nothing surprises me. Honestly, nothing surprises me. ZITA: “I have no answers. He - he was either beyond confident, maybe he wanted to be caught… VO: In February this year, almost five years after his arrest, a jury convicted Smith on 14 charges, including murder, and sexual assault. ERIN: ‘Do you still love Brian, and can you forgive him?’ ZITA: “I can’t answer that now, I’ve got to be honest with you.” VO: The families of Smith’s victims now await justice: he’ll be sentenced for his crime later this month. ZITA: “Brian didn’t just kill two women - the impact on everyone went beyond those two women. As a family, we have so much - how can I put it - their families have lost so much, but we’ve also lost someone - because we lost the Brian we knew. This isn't Brian. It’s not Brian.” ZITA: “Honestly… the only way Brian will leave prison is in a box, it’s that simple.” —------------------------------ PROMOS: PROMO 1: PRESENTER: He's been convicted of the so-called memory card murders in Anchorage, Alaska. But police suspect, it doesn't end there. BYTE ADRIAN ZOOM: “I asked them ‘why?’ Why they were interviewing me? And they said Brian had allegedly told his cellmates when he was in the US that he had murdered many women and he had never been caught.” PRESENTER: An alleged jail cell confession has authorities looking into long forgotten cold cases in SA. —---------------------------------- PROMO 2: PRESENTER: A South African convicted of two gruesome murders in Anchorage, Alaska awaits sentencing... BYTE ZITA: “We were horrified. To taunt someone when they are busy… Yeah, it was horrific. That hit me solidly. There was no getting away from it. He was as guilty as guilty can be. PRESENTER: We track his origins in the Eastern Cape and trace the makings of a murderer in the United States. —---------------------------- PROMO 3: PRESENTER: Found guilty of two murders in Alaska, the United States... The culprit was born here in rural Eastern Cape... WAYNE: “When I look at pictures of him on the news channels, his eyes are just - they've got this wild look in them. It’s not the look I know. It’s not the same person. He just looks angry, aggressive, and that’s not the person that I knew.” PRESENTER: What drove him to commit cold-blooded murder 17,000 kilometres away? And what trail of secrets did he leave in South Africa?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): He was an unsuspecting South African, building a new life in Alaska. Then he confessed to two grisly murders, which he documented for the Dark Web.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In February 2024, an Alaskan court found Brian Steven Smith (52) guilty of 14 charges - including two counts of murder, sexual assault, and torture. To the outside world, Brianwas your quintessential ‘nice guy’ - pleasant, quiet, standoffish, and awkward at times but his colleagues put that down to him being a non-Alaskan native. But behind closed doors, he was a man who frequently spoke of his deeply-rooted racist beliefs, was a regular on depraved chat sites on the dark web, and made snuff films. This is a story of the ‘meek’ man turned murderer, who left South Africa to pursue love, and now finds himself facing two life sentences for two brutal murders.
metadata.Summary: Brian Steven Smith, originally from Komani in the Eastern Cape, awaits sentencing for the murders of two native Alaskan women in Anchorage, Alaska in 2018 and 2019 respectively. Now experts believe he may be connected to a series of unsolved murders in SA after he confessed to more killings. Brian documented one of his murders - making 12 videos and taking 39 pictures of himself raping, torturing and murdering one of his victims. He narrated his actions in the videos as if to an audience, saying: "In my movies, people always die," and "People need to know when they're being serial-killed." This story will delve into the man behind the murders, looking at Brian's life growing up and living in the Eastern Cape, as well as his online persona. It will also tell the stories of his victims, and the families they've now left behind.
metadata.Further information: Sentencing is scheduled for July 12 and 19. He faces 30 to 99 years behind bars for killing Abouchuk, but will get the mandatory maximum of 99 years in prison for Henry’s death because jurors determined that there was an aggravating factor: He subjected her to substantial physical torture.
